chunks: Muhammad ibn Sinan narrated from Dawud al-Riqqi, from Abu Hamza al-Thumali, who said, 'I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) say:'

Verily Allah, the Almighty, made among His creatures some who are worthy of goodness (al-ma'ruf). He made them love goodness and love doing it. He enjoined upon those who seek goodness that they should refer to them and that they should fulfill it, just as He made rain flow easily to the arid land to bring it to life and cause its inhabitants to thrive.

And verily Allah made among His creatures some who are enemies of goodness. He made them detest goodness and hate doing it. He forbade those who seek goodness from referring to them and prevented them from fulfilling it, just as He prevents rain from falling on the arid land to destroy its inhabitants through it.
And what Allah forgives is greater [than what He punishes].

key_terms.قَضَاهُ: He fulfilled it / He carried it out

ai.seo_question: How does the Imam describe the divine distinction between those who facilitate and those who obstruct goodness?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) elucidates the divine distribution of receptivity to goodness (al-ma'ruf), contrasting those whose hearts are softened to receive it with those whose hearts are hardened against it. This narration employs the metaphor of rain to illustrate how spiritual vitality or desolation depends on one's inherent disposition, a concept central to Shia discussions on fitrah (innate nature) and divine decree. The concluding emphasis on Allah's forgiveness exceeding His punishment aligns with the Shia theological principle of 'Adb al-Karam' (Divine Generosity), offering hope even to those obstructed by their own nature.
